MEMORY (before this story): At twenty-two I bought the old boathouse on the East Landing with six years of saved fares. The roof leaked and the slip was half silted, but it was mine and nobody else's. I spent that autumn mending the roof and digging out the slip. It has a berth for the Heron, a net loft reached by a ladder, and a small spare room I have hardly used. I have lived there ever since.

What I did: I climb the inn's back stair for the first time, all the way to the top of the house, and go in at Oren's door. Then I said 'What is in the sacks?' Then I said 'The council has taken my evening trade and has me in its fines book once. Twice and they take the Heron.' Then I said 'Three nights' fares. And if they take her, you buy me another.' Then I put my hands in my coat pockets and look at the green glass instead of at him. What happened: I was standing -- standing in Oren Dask's workshop at the top of the Lantern Inn with my back to the door. The air carried hot solder, lamp oil and sawdust. How I came into it: uneasy, tempted, guarded.

MEMORY (23 beats ago): What I witnessed: I saw Ilse Harrow open the chapel house door before I could knock, already in her dark good dress with her hair pinned tight. I saw her take the oilcloth bundle from me, fold the cloth back and lay both hands flat on the ledger's cover. I heard Ilse Harrow say: "You'll not come up to the hall with me. No. I know. You never have, for any of it." What I did: I said 'I do not go to council business, Ilse. I will be at the landing when you come down.' Then I fold the oilcloth back over the corner of the ledger so the damp cannot get at it. Then I hold her by both shoulders for a moment and let her go. What happened: I heard Ilse Harrow say: "The landing, then. Wait for me there." I saw her shut the door, and her lamp move away inside. I was standing -- standing on the chapel house step in the dark before dawn with my hands empty. The air carried a hard cold and tallow from the chapel. How I came into it: protectiveness, tense, hopeful.

MEMORY (262 beats ago): What I witnessed: Half the stalls were up in the market square and the rest still under canvas weighted with stones. The baker's woman lifted two loaves off her board for me. I heard a seller say: "The chapel lost a dozen slates and the sexton's up his ladder already." Wren bought a stoppered bottle of ink at the next stall and held it up to the light. I heard Wren say: "The good ink. The map has earned it after last night." What I did: I said 'Two loaves. And a bundle of candles from the chandler, and grease for the lines.' Then I count my coins out onto the board. Then I put the loaves in my basket under a cloth. Then I said 'That is the last of the week's fares gone. The curfew halves my crossings and the river has had the rest.' What happened: I was standing -- standing at the baker's board in the market square with the basket on my arm. I heard Tobin say: "Did they say my name?" I heard Tobin say: "Then it'll be on paper in every village up the toll road by the end of the week." What I did: I said 'They said it. Tobin Reyes, twenty-eight, thin, a torn blue coat. They didn't find a hair of you.' Then I set down the pot of stew and my old grey blanket. Then I said 'One more night out here. They've searched the boathouse, so it's the safest place on the landing, but not while they're drinking at the inn.' Then I put the blanket round his shoulders and go before the light does. What happened: I was standing -- standing at the hut door with the last light going red over the reeds. The air carried cold mud and stew. How I came into it: protective, weary, grim.

They're still counting. The sexton says the stores are short by whole cartloads." I heard Ilse Harrow say: "And they say Oren Dask's gone downriver on the Moth. Has he sent any word back, Mara? To anyone?" What I did: I said 'No word from him. The innkeeper says he paid to the end of the month and took his glass and his tools.' Then I sit down on the bench under the window beside her. Then I said 'You put the ledger in their hands. Whatever they answer, that part is done, and it was right.' What happened: I heard Ilse Harrow say: "You kept it dry for me. Thank you, Mara." I could not answer that. I have told Ilse three lies this autumn -- that I had seen no one round the boathouse, that Tobin was my cousin from downriver, and where I was one night -- and she thanked me for keeping her ledger safe. I was sitting -- sitting on the bench beside Ilse with my hands between my knees. The air carried cold chapel stone and her mending wool. How I came into it: guilt, tenderness, sadness.
